items.text: A Michigan fire insurance policy is silent on actual cash value coverage. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(a), what is the statutory minimum the policy must still provide?
A. Actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss — MCL 500.2833(1)(a) requires, at minimum, coverage for the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss.

A family carries furniture out of a burning house to save it, and it sits in the yard for 3 days before it can be moved indoors, getting rained on. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(b), is that rain damage covered?

D. Yes, the statute requires pro rata coverage for 5 days for property removed to preserve it from a covered peril — MCL 500.2833(1)(b) requires pro rata coverage for 5 days for insured property removed to another location to preserve it from damage by a covered peril.
An insurer discovers the insured intentionally lied about a prior fire loss on the application. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(c), on what basis may the policy be void?
C. Misrepresentation, fraud, or concealment — MCL 500.2833(1)(c) allows the policy to be void on the basis of misrepresentation, fraud, or concealment.
A homeowner in Wayne County wants to cancel their Michigan fire policy mid-term. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(h), can they do this, and what is the minimum the insurer keeps?

D. Yes, and the insurer keeps the pro rata premium for expired time or $25.00, whichever is greater — MCL 500.2833(1)(h) lets the insured cancel at any time, with a minimum earned premium of the pro rata amount for expired time or $25.00, whichever is greater.
An insurer decides to cancel a Michigan fire policy mid-term. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(i), what must the mailed cancellation notice include?

C. A statement that unearned excess premium, if not tendered, will be refunded on demand — MCL 500.2833(1)(i) requires the cancellation notice to state that the excess premium, if not tendered, will be refunded on demand.

A bank holds a mortgage on a fire-damaged Michigan home and is named as loss payee but not as an insured. The homeowner never files proof of loss. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(j), what happens to the bank's claim?

B. The bank, on notice, must render its own proof of loss within 60 days — MCL 500.2833(1)(j) requires the mortgagee, on notice, to render proof of loss within 60 days after the notice if the insured fails to do so.
An insurer pays a mortgagee on a Michigan fire claim but denies liability to the homeowner-mortgagor. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(j), what right does the insurer gain?

C. Subrogation to the mortgagee's recovery rights, capped at the amount paid, without impairing the mortgagee's own right to sue — MCL 500.2833(1)(j) subrogates the insurer to the mortgagee's rights of recovery (contract and tort) to the extent of the loss paid, without impairing the mortgagee's own suit rights.
A homeowner's fire loss is also covered under a second policy from a different carrier. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(k), how is the first insurer's liability limited?
D. It owes only its pro rata share alongside the other insurance — MCL 500.2833(1)(k) caps the insurer's liability at its pro rata share with other insurance covering the same peril.
An insured and insurer disagree on the amount of loss after a Macomb County house fire. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(m), who may demand appraisal, and by when must each side name its own appraiser?

B. Either party may demand it, and each must name its appraiser within 20 days of the written demand — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) lets either party make a written demand for appraisal, with each side naming its own appraiser within 20 days of receiving that demand.
Two appraisers in a Michigan fire claim cannot agree on an umpire after 15 days. What happens next under MCL 500.2833(1)(m)?

B. Either party may ask a circuit court judge, in the county of the loss or property, to select an umpire — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) allows either the insured or insurer to ask a circuit court judge in the relevant county to select an umpire when the two appraisers cannot agree within 15 days.

An appraisal panel in a Michigan fire claim reaches a split decision: one appraiser and the umpire sign a written agreement on the amount of loss, but the second appraiser refuses to sign. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(m), does the amount stand?

C. Yes, a written agreement signed by any 2 of the 3 sets the amount of loss — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) states that a written agreement signed by any 2 of the 3 (the two appraisers or one appraiser and the umpire) sets the amount of the loss.
An insurer decides, instead of paying cash, to send its own crew to rebuild a fire-damaged Michigan home. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(n), is this allowed?
A. Yes, the insurer may repair, replace, rebuild, or take the property instead of paying cash — MCL 500.2833(1)(n) gives the insurer the option to repair, replace, rebuild, or take the property.
A homeowner wants to hand over the burned remains of their home to the insurer and be paid as if it were a total loss, without further claim documentation. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(o), can they do this?
A. No, the statute says there can be no abandonment to the insurer of any property — MCL 500.2833(1)(o) states there can be no abandonment to the insurer of any property.

An insured in a small Michigan township (population under 425,000 county, no 50,000-plus municipality) submits proof of the amount of loss on a fire claim, and the township has opted into MCL 500.2845's escrow program. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(p), does the insurer still owe payment within 30 days of that proof?

B. No, the 30-day rule is expressly subject to MCL 500.2845's escrow-withholding mechanics — MCL 500.2833(1)(p) pays the loss within 30 days of proof of amount of loss except as otherwise provided in section 2845, so a qualifying 2845 escrow delay is not a violation.

A homeowner in Grand Rapids suffers a fire loss on March 1. They notify their insurer of the loss the same day. The insurer does not formally deny liability until 18 months later. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(q), has the insured's right to sue expired?

A. No, the 1-year clock was tolled from the notice of loss until the insurer's formal denial, so it has not yet started running toward expiration — MCL 500.2833(1)(q) tolls the suit-limitation clock from notice of loss until the insurer formally denies liability; since the insurer had not formally denied until 18 months in, the clock had not been running.
Under MCL 500.2833(1)(s), when does a Michigan fire insurance policy become effective?
D. At 12:01 a.m. standard time at the location of the property — MCL 500.2833(1)(s) sets the effective time as 12:01 a.m., standard time, at the location of the property involved.
A student cites 'MCL 500.2832' as the current statute setting Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions. What is wrong with this cite?

A. 500.2832 was repealed effective January 1, 1992; the current mandatory-provisions statute is MCL 500.2833 — MCL 500.2832 (former standard fire policy) was repealed effective January 1, 1992, by the same 1990 Act 305 that added the current MCL 500.2833.

A fire loss occurs on a home in a city within a county of 500,000 people. The municipality has an active escrow program. Which statute governs the withholding, and what was the maximum withholding for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026 per DIFS Bulletin 2026-16-INS?

C. MCL 500.2227, $24,096 — A county of 500,000 falls under MCL 500.2227's larger-population band; Bulletin 2026-16-INS lists $24,096 as the maximum withholding for July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, one period before the current $25,090 figure.
Under MCL 500.2845, a small township's fire-loss escrow sits with the treasurer for 150 days with no reasonable proof of repair or demolition shown. What can the township do under subsection (7)?

C. It may use the retained proceeds to secure, repair, or demolish the structure and clear the property, returning any unused portion to the insured — MCL 500.2845(7) allows the municipality, once the 120-day proof window passes without reasonable proof, to use the retained proceeds itself to secure, repair, or demolish the structure and clear the property, returning unused funds to the insured.

A restoration contractor wants to speed up a homeowner's disputed Michigan fire claim by personally demanding an appraisal from the carrier and negotiating the umpire selection for a fee. Is this consistent with MCL 500.2833(1)(m) and MCL 500.1222?

D. No, appraisal is the insured's statutory right to demand; a contractor negotiating it for a fee risks unlicensed public adjusting under MCL 500.1222 — MCL 500.2833(1)(m) gives the appraisal-demand right to the insured or insurer, not a contractor; a contractor handling that negotiation for compensation risks the unlicensed-adjusting prohibition in MCL 500.1222.
